337.title: Upakosala and the fires (4.10–4.15)
337.hook: a student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and is never sent home; then the fires themselves begin to teach
337.howItsDone: In the traditional guru-shishya relationship, a Hindu student serves and lives with a teacher for years; some Hindu traditions also speak of an inner guide, and of the outer teacher as one who points the student inward.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bull, the fire, the swan and the diving bird, Satyakama's four unlikely teachers. Your line was the whole world teaches. Week two of year two begins.

Satyakama grows up and becomes a teacher himself, with a student of his own, Upakosala. For twelve years, Upakosala lives in his teacher's house and tends the sacred fires, morning and evening. Other students come, finish and are sent home. Not him. Then Satyakama leaves on a journey, still without teaching him, and Upakosala, the text says, is so sad he stops eating. The teacher's wife begs him to eat something. No, he says. I'm full of sorrow. And that's when the fires he's tended for twelve years start to talk.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS TENDING THE FIRES.` → `EVERYONE ELSE GOES HOME.` → `HE STOPS EATING.`

segments.voice: The fires confer among themselves. This student has served us well; let's teach him. Together they tell him: breath is Brahman. Ka is Brahman. Kha is Brahman. Upakosala is honest: I understand breath is Brahman, but not ka and kha. Ka means joy, they explain, and kha means space, and they're one: the joy that is also space, the space that is also joy. Then each of the three fires teaches him about itself, and about the sun, the moon, the lightning, the waters. We've told you our part, they say. Your teacher will tell you the way. When Satyakama comes home, he looks at his student and says what was said to him years ago: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Upakosala, a little embarrassed, glances at the fires. Satyakama listens, then says: they told you about the worlds. I'll tell you the rest. As water doesn't cling to a lotus leaf, wrongdoing doesn't cling to one who knows this. And his teaching is this: the person you see in the eye, that is the self, that is Brahman, deathless and fearless. Notice the shape of it. The fires teach the outer things. The teacher points inward, to the one looking out through the eyes. The story keeps both: Upakosala needed his teacher, and he needed the fires. But where everything finally points is the seer inside.

segments.voice: Light a candle if you have one, or look at any small light, and watch it for a few breaths: the flicker, the color. Then gently notice that someone is seeing it. Don't try to find that someone; just rest in the fact of seeing, joy and space, ka and kha.
Upakosala, the student who tended the sacred fires for twelve years. The fires taught him about the world, and his teacher pointed him to the self within.
Your line: the teacher within. It's where Satyakama's teaching pointed. Day three hundred thirty-seven, done.

338.title: The five fires (5.4–5.9)
338.hook: a king asks a proud young scholar five questions he can't answer, and the answer turns out to be the whole cycle of life told as five fires
338.carry: rain to food to seed to person
338.howItsDone: Hindu rites of passage, from conception to cremation, are traditionally performed around a sacred fire, and cremation is treated in Hindu rites as a final offering into the fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upakosala, who tended the fires for twelve years. The fires taught him the worlds; his teacher pointed him to the seer in the eye. Your line was the teacher within.

A young man named Shvetaketu comes to the assembly of the Panchalas, where Pravahana Jaivali is king. The king asks: has your father taught you? Yes, sir. Then do you know where people go when they leave this world? No. How they come back? No. Why that other world never fills up? No. Five questions, five blanks. Shvetaketu goes home, stung: you told me you had taught me! His father admits he doesn't know either. So the father goes to the king himself and asks to be taught. And what the king teaches him is a picture of five fires.
screen: `FIVE QUESTIONS, FIVE BLANKS.` → `THE FATHER DOESN'T KNOW EITHER.` → `HE GOES TO THE KING.`

segments.voice: Go back to the sacrifice from the first day of this year: a fire, and an offering poured into it. The king says the whole world works like that. Five fires, five offerings. The first fire is the sky world up there. The gods pour in faith, and out of it comes Soma, the moon. The second fire is the rain cloud: Soma goes in, and out comes rain. The third is the earth: rain goes in, and out comes food, rice, barley, plants. The fourth is a man: food goes in, and out comes seed. The fifth is a woman: seed goes in, and out comes an embryo, a child on the way. Then the line the whole passage rests on: in the fifth offering, the waters come to be called a person. Rain to food to seed to person. You are, in this picture, weather that has been offered and transformed five times. And it doesn't stop at birth. The person lives, dies, and is placed on the funeral fire, the last fire, and the cycle turns again. The next chapter describes the paths the dead take from there, the way of the gods and the way of the ancestors. Notice two things. First, a king, a warrior, is teaching a priest; the text has the king say this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before. Second, the fire is everywhere: not only on the altar, but in clouds, soil, bodies and births. The ritual became a way to see the whole world.

Then feel yourself sitting here, made, the king would say, of offered rain.
Pancagni, the five fires: sky, rain cloud, earth, man and woman, each receiving an offering and giving something new, until the waters become a person.
Your line: rain to food to seed to person. Tomorrow, that father and son again. Until then.

339.title: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu: "you've studied twelve years — do you know That?" (6.1)
339.hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, proud and stiff, and his father asks him one question he can't answer
339.tomorrow: the clay, the gold, the iron
339.howItsDone: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya is one of the most studied texts in Hindu philosophy; Vedanta teachers often walk students through Uddalaka's lessons one at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pancagni, the king's five fires, and your line, rain to food to seed to person.
screen: `PANCAGNI — RAIN TO FOOD TO SEED TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: The front door opens. A young man comes home after twelve years away. He's twenty-four. He has memorized the Vedas. He walks in, the text says, swollen with pride, thinking himself very learned, a little stiff with it. Maybe you've met him. Maybe you've been him, home from the first year of college, correcting everyone at dinner. His father watches him for a while. Then he asks one question, and it isn't a test of memory. So begins the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the most studied in Hindu philosophy: a father, a son, and two weeks of lessons.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS.` → `SWOLLEN WITH PRIDE.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The father is Uddalaka Aruni, one of the great teachers of the Upanishads. The son is Shvetaketu, the same young man the king embarrassed yesterday. When Shvetaketu was twelve, his father sent him off to study with a warning: in our family, nobody is a brahmin just by birth. Go and learn. Now he's back, proud of all he knows. And his father asks: since you think so much of yourself, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. How could there be such a teaching, sir? The question isn't asking for one more fact; twelve years of facts are already in his head. It asks whether there's one thing that, once known, makes everything else make sense. A key, not another room. The Upanishads often just call what that key opens That. And the father is gentle. He doesn't mock. He uses a word he'll repeat through all the lessons ahead: somya, my dear, the way you'd talk to someone you love. Then he begins to teach with things from the kitchen and the garden: clay, salt, honey, a seed. Nine times, he'll close a lesson with the same three words.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS EARLIER, A WARNING.` · `THE UNHEARD BECOMES HEARD.` · `A KEY, NOT ANOTHER ROOM.` · `SOMYA, MY DEAR.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Let what you know come up, your job, your skills, your opinions, what you studied, and set each one down beside you like books on a table; you can pick them all up later. For now, sit with empty hands, and let the father's question hang in the air, unanswered.
Somya, gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons, as he asks whether anyone taught him the one teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
Your line: the one thing worth knowing. Tomorrow, his first lesson: a lump of clay. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.

340.title: The clay, the gold, the iron — know one, know all (6.1)
340.hook: by knowing one lump of clay, the father says, you know everything made of clay: the pot is only a name
340.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers of different schools use Uddalaka's clay, gold and iron as a teaching example, and the clay-and-pot image returns often in later Hindu philosophy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: somya, my dear, and a proud son facing one question. Your line was the one thing worth knowing.

Look along a kitchen shelf in India and there may well be clay on it. A water pot. A cup for chai, thrown away after one use. A lamp for the evening. A plate, a jar, a tile. Different shapes, different names, different jobs. Shvetaketu has just asked how there could possibly be one teaching that makes everything known. His father doesn't answer with a theory. He points at the pots.
screen: `A POT, A CUP, A LAMP, A JAR.` → `DIFFERENT NAMES, DIFFERENT JOBS.` → `HE POINTS AT THE POTS.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: my dear, just as by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known, the change is only a name, a matter of words, and the truth is just clay. In Sanskrit, the end of that line runs: vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam, mrittiketyeva satyam. Then he says it twice more. By one gold ornament, everything made of gold is known; the truth is just gold. By one nail-cutter, everything made of iron is known; the truth is just iron. Think about what he's claiming. A pot is real. You can carry water in it. But pot is the name for a shape the clay has taken for a while. Break the pot, and nothing has gone out of existence. The clay is still there; it just doesn't answer to pot anymore. So if you understand clay, you understand every pot, cup and lamp at once, including ones you'll never see. Know the clay, and the names stop confusing you. Over the next lessons, the clay will turn out to be something much bigger: what Uddalaka calls Being, the one stuff under every name. Hindu schools read this line in different ways. Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, hears the many names as appearance, with only the one ultimately real. Other Vedanta schools, like Ramanuja's, hear the pots as real forms of the one clay. Both come back to this lump of clay.

341.title: In the beginning, Being alone (6.2)
341.hook: the father goes back to the beginning: there was only Being, one, without a second
341.carry: it thought: let me be many
341.howItsDone: Uddalaka's opening line, 'Being alone, one without a second', is quoted again and again in Hindu philosophy, and Vedanta teachers use ekam evadvitiyam as a short summary of their teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the clay. Know one lump, and you know every pot. Your line was know the clay.

But what was there before? Before Grandma, before the dinosaurs, before the world? Kids ask it at bedtime. Philosophers ask it for a living. The Upanishads ask it too. Uddalaka has told his son that under every pot there's clay. Now Shvetaketu needs to know what the clay of everything is. So the father goes back to the beginning, with a creation story short enough for bedtime.
screen: `BUT WHAT WAS THERE BEFORE?` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `THE CLAY OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka begins: sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam. In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Sat: Being, what is. Then he takes on a rival view head-on. Some say that in the beginning there was non-being, and Being came out of it. But how could something come from nothing? No, my dear. In the beginning there was Being. Then the turn that gives today's line. That Being thought: let me be many. Let me grow forth. It sends out heat. The heat, in turn, thinks: let me be many, and sends out water. That's why, Uddalaka says, when a person is hot or grieving, they sweat or weep: water comes out of heat. The water thinks the same thought, and sends out food. That's why, wherever it rains, there's plenty to eat. Heat, water, food: the three basic stuffs everything else will be made of. Fire, water, food: Uddalaka keeps building big ideas out of the kitchen. And notice the motive. The text names nothing outside Being that makes it act. It simply thinks, let me be many. Later Hindu thinkers read that line in more than one way. Some hear the one truly becoming the many. Others hear the one appearing as many while staying one. The text just tells the story, and leaves the rest for the lessons to come.

342.title: The three colors — red, white, black (6.4)
342.hook: look at a flame: the red is heat, the white is water, the black is food, and the 'fire' itself turns out to be a name
342.tomorrow: food, water, heat become mind, breath, speech
342.howItsDone: The idea that everything is woven of a few basic strands runs through later Hindu thought, including the three gunas of Samkhya and the Gita; some scholars see Uddalaka's three colors as an early forerunner of these ideas, though the link is debated.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, Being alone, one without a second, becoming heat, water and food. Your line was it thought: let me be many.

Light a match and look closely at the flame. It isn't one color. There's a reddish glow, a bright whitish part, and a dark edge where the stick is burning down. Usually it's just fire, blown out before it reaches your fingers. Uddalaka, teaching his son Shvetaketu, looks at the same flame and sees yesterday's creation story, still going on, right there in the colors.
screen: `LIGHT A MATCH.` → `NOT ONE COLOR.` → `THE CREATION STORY, STILL GOING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Being became heat, water and food. Now Uddalaka says Being entered into them with the living self, gave them name and form, and wove each one together with the other two, so that everything is a braid of three. Then he points to a fire. The red color of fire is the form of heat. The white is the form of water. The black is the form of food, of earth. And then something startling: so the fireness of fire has gone. The change is only a name, a matter of words. The truth is the three colors. That's the clay line from two days ago, word for word, except now the pot is a flame. He does the same with the sun, the moon and lightning: red, white and black in each, and sun-ness, moon-ness, lightning-ness only names. Then he mentions the old teachers. The great householders of old knew this, he says, and so they said: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or thought or known. Whatever they saw that was red, they knew as heat; white, as water; black, as food. Nobody's claiming this is how a modern lab would describe a flame. The point is a way of seeing. Behind the bright, separate things of the world, Uddalaka sees a few simple strands, and behind those strands, the one Being they came from. Look behind the colors, and the world gets simpler, not smaller.

Trivrit, threefold, braided of three. Red for heat, white for water, black for food: Uddalaka's way of seeing every fire, sun and moon this way.
Your line: behind the colors. A few strands, and one Being behind them. Day three hundred forty-two, done.

segments.voice: Yesterday: trivrit, red for heat, white for water, black for food. Your line was behind the colors. Today ends week two of year two.

Four o'clock, and no lunch. The same email, read three times, and it still won't go in. A short temper, a foggy head. Then someone hands over a sandwich, and ten minutes later the email makes sense. That's usually filed under being hungry. Uddalaka files it under the mind, and turns it into a test, with his own son as the subject.

segments.voice: Here's what happens to the three stuffs once they're inside you, Uddalaka says. Food, when eaten, divides into three. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Water divides the same way: the coarsest leaves, the middle becomes blood, the finest becomes breath. Heat, taken in through oils and ghee, divides too: its coarsest part becomes bone, the middle marrow, the finest speech. So mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat. Shvetaketu says, please, tell me more. So his father gives him an experiment. Don't eat for fifteen days. Drink water as you like, since breath is made of water. Shvetaketu fasts, comes back, and his father says: recite the Vedas. He can't. Nothing comes, sir. His father gives a picture: when a great fire has burned down to one ember the size of a firefly, it can't burn much. But add straw, and it blazes again. Go eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and now he can answer every question. The mind is made of food, my dear. Seven days this week, in one breath: Upakosala and the fires. The king's five fires. The proud son and the one question. The clay. Being alone, which thought, let me be many. The three colors. And today, food becoming mind. The Chandogya keeps refusing to separate the sacred from the stomach.
